<Reviewer 1>: 2. Moreover, the interpretation of what is being measured magnetically
requires further clarification. The dislocation structures that evolve during fatigue can
vary substantially in nature, yet the proposed technique appears to treat them
equivalently, potentially overlooking key distinctions in how different dislocation
configurations influence fatigue behavior. For instance, dislocation annihilation, slip
reversibility, an important mechanism that may still lead to micro-damage, is unlikely
to be captured by the magnetic signal, despite its relevance to fatigue failure.
Response:
In the process of material fatigue, microscopic evolution mechanisms such as
dislocation annihilation and slip reversibility indeed have significant effects on fatigue
failure. Dislocation annihilation typically occurs when two spatially adjacent
dislocations with opposite Burgers vectors cause lattice distortions (such as
compressive and tensile regions) that cancel each other out, thereby restoring the lattice
to a state of lower distortion. However, the changes in atomic spacing caused by
dislocations near the annihilation site may be difficult to fully recover.
Slip reversibility refers to whether dislocations generated by slip under forward
loading can return along the original path during reverse loading in cyclic deformation,
thereby restoring the local lattice to its initial state. The key lies in whether dislocations
can strictly retreat along their original path, which can be judged by whether the local
atomic spacing can fully recover: under cyclic loading, if the lattice distortions caused
by forward slip can be eliminated through reverse slip, the atomic spacing may be
restored; otherwise, if dislocation retreat is impeded, the atomic spacing will change,
leading to residual plastic strain that gradually accumulates into fatigue damage.
Regarding the fatigue fracture mechanism in materials, we believe that: the
interlamellar atomic spacing to a certain extent determines the strength of interlamellar
bonding and interlamellar exchange interactions; when the material system is fixed,
atomic spacing becomes the dominant variable regulating both; the essence of fatigue
fracture is the continuous weakening of interlamellar bonding strength as the spacing
increases, and once the bonding strength falls below a critical threshold of the applied
load, fracture occurs immediately; through the spin-correlation amplification effect,
the
MagDrift signal amplifies this microscopic process of weakened bonding strength into
an observable macroscopic response.
The above represents our current understanding of this issue. If there are any
oversights or shortcomings, we sincerely invite your feedback and suggestions.
To further clarify the interpretation of the magnetic measurement results. The
revised text in the manuscript is provided below (lines 108-141): “The fatigue
behaviours of materials manifest microscopically as the formation of various
dislocation structures (e.g., persistent slip bands (PSBs), dislocation annihilation,
reversible slip, and the ratcheting effect), which are characteristic features of localized
plastic deformation under cyclic loading (Fig. 1a). At the microscopic level, the
formation of these structures originates from the motion, interaction, and accumulation
of dislocations at the nanoscale within the crystal lattice, gradually evolving into visible
slip bands or other defect structures4. This evolutionary process is highly nonlinear and
strongly dependent on crystal structures, loading conditions, and environmental factors.
For instance, in face-centred cubic (FCC) metals, dislocations undergo rearrangement
through reversible slip (where partial dislocations return along their original paths under
alternating loads, leading to partial damage recovery) and dislocation annihilation
(where dislocations with opposite signs meet and cancel each other out). This initially
results in the formation of vein-like structures, which further develop into cellular
structures. In contrast, for body-centred cubic (BCC) metals or objects under high-
stress amplitude conditions, the ratcheting effect (the unidirectional accumulation of
strain under asymmetric cyclic loading) becomes more pronounced, promoting
irreversible and rapid dislocation accumulation.
The nucleation and motion of dislocations are associated with the weakening of
interatomic bonding forces18 (interatomic cohesion; Fig. 1a). During cyclic loading, a
localized stress concentration reduces the interatomic bonding strength, facilitating
dislocation nucleation and slip processes25. This slip is not always uniform; its degree
of localization can be characterized by slip planarity. Higher planarity indicates that the
slip is concentrated on fewer planes, making it easier to form sharp persistent slip bands
(PSBs). The interfaces between these bands and the matrix become high-risk regions
for crack initiation. In some alloys, microscopic plasticity may also appear in the form
of fatigue shear bands, which are intensely localized shear bands that traverse grains.
Their formation is closely related to microstructural anisotropy.
Therefore, fatigue damage in materials is essentially a multiscale evolutionary
process spanning the atomic, microscopic, and macroscopic dimensions. From a
microscopic perspective, this process is located within the damage concentration zone.
This region consists of multiple atomic layers within the fatigue-affected zone and
contains a series of microscopic defect clusters that influence the interlamellar atomic
spacing (here, “interlamellar” refers to the collective set of all the atoms contained
within a three-dimensional irregular thin section that is perpendicular to the direction
of structural loading). Throughout this process, damage to the interlamellar atomic
bonding force continuously accumulates. When this force falls below the stress induced
by the applied load, material fracture occurs. Hence, changes in the interlamellar atomic
bonding force can serve as indicators for characterizing the fatigue states of materials.”
Revised text in the manuscript (lines 146-147): “These challenges are particularly
pronounced when complex transient processes such as dynamic dislocation annihilation,
reorganization and reversible slip are involved.”
<Reviewer 1>: 3. The influence of loading conditions is also insufficiently addressed.
As an example, under ratcheting conditions, dislocation density may increase
significantly, but the associated damage mechanisms can differ from those occurring
under non-ratcheting fatigue. Such distinctions are critical and should be reflected in
the analysis.
Response:
The differences in the fatigue damage mechanisms between ratcheting and non-
ratcheting effects are important for accurately analyzing material fatigue behavior. Our
discussion of this issue in the original manuscript was insufficient. The following is our
understanding of the dislocation behavior under different loading conditions:
The essence of the ratcheting effect is the combined effect of gradual attenuation
of the bonding force and incomplete dislocation annihilation caused by the irreversible
net increase of atomic spacing under cyclic loading. The core of non-ratcheting
behavior lies in the reversible elastic oscillation of atomic spacing to maintain bonding
stability and realize full annihilation through dislocation reverse slip. Although the
microscopic mechanisms of ratcheting and non-ratcheting effects are different, their
essence is related to atomic spacing.

There are some differences in plastic deformation mechanism between pure

average measurement methods. We noticed that the previous description of the
theoretical model was oversimplified, and there was a lack of clarity in the
interpretation of the basic principles, which may lead to a misunderstanding of the

The essence of spin correlation amplification technology is not spatial average
measurement. Its essence is to transform the spin correlation change triggered by the
change of interlamellar atomic spacing into a macro measurable MagDrift signal
through the effect of multiple amplification. Its core mechanism is the multiple
amplification mechanism dominated by local damage.
Universal response mechanism to different material damage modes: Although
regular and coarse persistent slip bands (PSBs) are usually formed in pure metals (such
as nickel), plastic strain localization in high-strength alloys (such as high-strength steel)
tends to be more dispersed or discontinuous in the form of microstrip, grain boundary
slip or phase boundary cracking due to the existence of barriers such as grain boundary
and second phase particle. However, whether the specific microscopic morphology is
persistent slip band (PSB) or other types of strain localization regions, the physical
essence behind it is due to lattice distortion, the increase of atomic spacing and the
weakening of atomic bonding force. The change of spin correlation is a direct physical
response highly sensitive to these microstructure changes. Therefore, the detection
target of this technology can be directly traced to the attenuation of atomic bonding
force, which is unified in physical nature and does not differ from PSB or other damage
modes.

effect of the spin correlation amplification of the exchange interaction (magnetic
moment). The local nature of fatigue damage will have a dominant effect on the global
change of MagDrift signal. For a detailed explanation, please refer to <Reviewer 1>:

<Reviewer 1>: 18. In fatigue, strain hardening or softening phenomena often occur,
altering the dislocation structure over time. The manuscript does not discuss how these
effects would influence MagDrift or whether the method can differentiate between them.
Response:
Cyclic hardening and cyclic softening are two typical responses of metal materials
under fatigue loading. Cyclic hardening shows that the ability of the material to resist
deformation is enhanced, and its macroscopic characteristic is that the dynamic stiffness
increases with time, which usually results from the increase of dislocation density and
its entanglement; On the contrary, cyclic softening shows that the material softens and
the dynamic stiffness decreases, and its microscopic mechanism is related to the
formation of low-energy dislocation structure by dislocation recombination.
We have drawn dynamic stiffness and MagDrift curves for representative
specimens of soft magnet iron, pure nickel, 45 steel and Q235 steel respectively (Fig.
12). It was found that all specimens exhibited initial cyclic hardening stage (although
the duration was short), then entered a stable cyclic softening stage, and finally showed
accelerated softening phenomenon in the failure stage. In terms of magnetic response,
the dynamic stiffness of soft magnet iron, 45 steel and Q235 steel increased at first and
then increased steadily at the beginning of loading, showing cyclic hardening, while the
MagDrift had no sudden change in this process, showing an accelerated upward trend,
rising steadily in the stable softening stage, and changing rapidly with the softening
acceleration at the failure stage. On the contrary, the MagDrift of Pure Nickel shows an
accelerated downward trend during cyclic hardening, and it also accelerates with
softening acceleration in the failure stage.
Fig. 12. Comparative analysis of dynamic stiffness and MagDrift of four materials. a, Dynamic
stiffness and MagDrift diagram of soft magnetic iron specimen under the condition of maximum
stress of 425 MPa and fatigue failure life of 97 K. b, Dynamic stiffness and MagDrift diagram of
pure nickel specimen under the condition of maximum stress of 430 MPa and fatigue failure life of
maximum stress of 560 MPa and fatigue failure life of 226 K. d, Dynamic stiffness and MagDrift
diagram of Q235 steel specimen under the condition of maximum stress of 520 MPa and fatigue
failure life of 230 K.
The above results show that different materials may affect the response sensitivity
of magnetic signal to micro plastic deformation, but the synergistic behavior of
MagDrift and stiffness change plays an auxiliary role in distinguishing the cyclic
hardening and softening processes.

Response:
In the process of material fatigue research, we focus on the quantum of the
synchronous attenuation of bonding force driven by the change of interlamellar atomic
spacing. The evolution of dislocation behavior (dislocation annihilation, slip,
recombination) can trigger the response of electron spin correlation amplification as
long as its essence is related to the change of atomic spacing. Although the slip planarity
modulates the spatial distribution of bit stagger, its core effect on fatigue still leads to
the attenuation of bonding force through the increase of atomic spacing. The MagDrift
signal is directly related to the interlamellar bonding force and the exchange interaction.
The change of the interlamellar atoms spacing becomes the dominant variable to control
the strength of the two, which transcends the microscopic mechanism limitation of the
slip geometry difference.

<Reviewer 1>: 20. The approach is reminiscent of nonlinear acoustic techniques used
to monitor dislocation density evolution. However, as in those methods, without spatial
correlation at the microstructural level, dislocation density alone cannot reliably predict
fatigue life. For example, in the Very High Cycle Fatigue (VHCF) regime, no
measurable macroscopic strain evolution is typically observed, and this method would
likely fail to detect damage evolution. Similarly, when fatigue is initiated at large
defects, the deformation is highly localized and may not be captured by spatially
averaged signals.
Response:
Although both spin correlation amplification and nonlinear acoustic techniques
can be used for material damage detection, their physical principles and response
mechanisms are essentially different.
Nonlinear acoustic technology relies on nonlinear distortion of lattice strain field:
dislocation evolution under cyclic loading or microcracks lead to high-order harmonics
in acoustic wave propagation, and the damage degree is inversed by measuring acoustic
nonlinear parameters (such as β coefficient). The response of this method is essentially
due to the enhancement of phonon defect scattering caused by periodic lattice damage.
Its signal strength is modulated by macroscopic parameters such as material density
and elastic modulus, and it has no direct ability to perceive atomic scale changes.
In contrast, spin correlation amplification technology achieves detection by
capturing the electron spin correlation effect caused by changes in atomic spacing in
ferromagnetic materials: when fatigue leads to an increase in interlamellar atomic
spacing, the attenuation of interlamellar exchange interactions triggers directional
deflection of the spin magnetic moment. This local perturbation is exponentially
amplified through the spin correlation chain and ultimately manifests as measurable
magnetic signal changes at the macroscopic level. Its core advantage lies in its
sensitivity to electronic changes and its nonlinear signal gain characteristics, which
amplify quantum effects as they pass through the fatigue dislocation layer.
Effectiveness of high cycle fatigue
In order to verify the effectiveness of this technology in VHCF scenario, we added
high cycle fatigue test: 45 steel, the loading parameters were consistent with the original
(Methods), and the maximum stress was 480 MPa. After two weeks of continuous
loading, the experiment was forced to stop after 22.17 million times due to time.
In Fig. 13, no macroscopic measurable evolution of displacement and
displacement amplitude is observed, but the magnetic signal has a macroscopic
measurable evolution, especially the MagDrift signal, which shows a clear downward
trend, indicating that the interlamellar bonding force is gradually weakening to some
extent. This confirms that under high-cycle fatigue conditions, MagDrift can still
achieve early damage warning by capturing the gradual attenuation of the atomic
bonding force.

We found that the absolute value of the average slope of the M-N curves for the

curves may represent a macroscopic manifestation of electron cloud overlap in
ferromagnetic metals. Therefore, in this paper, we adopted the average slope of the four

The MagDrift metric is designed as a differential measure, which inherently

perturbations.
Furthermore, these disturbances typically vary very little within a stress cycle, and
their impact on the magnetic strength peak-to-peak value is far smaller than their impact
on the absolute magnetic field strength. Therefore, the magnetic strength peak-to-peak
value exhibits good self-compensating characteristics, better reflecting changes in the
material's internal state compared to the absolute field strength value, and reducing
errors introduced by factors such as zero-point drift in the measurement system. This is
also a key reason why the paper adopts the MagDrift as the representative index for
evaluating the material's fatigue state.
Interference resistance test verification based on MagDrift self-compensation
mechanism
We supplemented the fatigue loading tests under various human-induced
disturbances to further verify the rationality of selecting the magnetic strength peak-to-
peak value as the representative index in the paper.
This experiment mainly simulates various possible influencing factors by applying
various artificial disturbances during the fatigue loading process. These include
temperature noise, changes in environmental magnetic field strength, poor contact in
the test data acquisition instrument channels, and electrical noise interference from
high-power electrical appliances. The corresponding magnetic strength and MagDrift
change data under these artificial disturbance factors are shown in Fig. 17.
Fig. 17. Comparison of magnetic field strength and MagDrift data after fatigue test
interference. The shaded areas indicate periods of data acquisition system disconnection. Sudden
changes or jumps in magnetic field strength data during this experiment were primarily attributed
to factors such as temperature noise, fluctuations in ambient magnetic fields, and electromagnetic
noise interference introduced by high-power equipment. In contrast, the MagDrift signal, leveraging
its inherent self-compensating mechanism, exhibits an intrinsic ability to suppress these interference
factors, thereby maintaining a more stable trend throughout the process.
As shown in the figure, the absolute magnetic field strength values of this test
specimen exhibit significant variations. These effects include data gaps in magnetic
field strength values and MagDrift data caused by poor contact in the data acquisition
instrument channels (shaded areas in the figure indicate where data was supplemented),
as well as fluctuations in absolute magnetic field values due to surrounding magnetic
field interference. However, owing to its inherent self-compensation capability, the
MagDrift data effectively mitigates the effects of these factors. Consequently, despite
some localized fluctuations, the MagDrift data demonstrates overall stability.
Finally, since MagDrift better reflects the fatigue process relative to absolute
magnetic field strength values, revealing changes in the material's internal fatigue state,
this paper employs MagDrift as the core metric for evaluating material fatigue
conditions.
In order to clarify why the paper chose MagDrift as a representative indicator, we
have supplemented the Methods section of the manuscript with the following
explanation: (lines 944-963): “MagDrift features a self-compensation ability.”

<Reviewer 2>: 4. In the “Fatigue Failure Warning” section (Line 373), the manuscript
states: “the Stage 2 system achieves 100% reliable early warning success rate.” What
is the specific criterion for determining whether the early warning is successful?
Response:
There are two specific criteria for determining successful early warning. First,
even when the material shows no visible cracks or macroscopic deformation, the
MagDrift index has already detected fatigue damage at the atomic scale through the
spin correlation amplification mechanism, and the MagDrift trend has shown a clear
fatigue fracture inflection point. At this point, the MagDrift inflection point is strongly
correlated with the final fracture.
On this basis, the warning mechanism used in the paper has captured the sudden
change characteristics of MagDrift and issued a fracture warning. Subsequently, even
after the material issued a warning, it could still safely bear thousands of external loads
on average, providing a critical buffer period for shutdown and maintenance. This also
solved the fatal flaw of traditional fatigue detection methods, which were “unable to
give fatigue failure warnings.”
We used this early warning mechanism to conduct fatigue fracture early warning
tests on all fatigue test specimens and found that the MagDrift curves of all 193 sets of
specimens showed obvious inflection points before fracture. Furthermore, all materials
were still able to safely withstand external loads for a period of time after the fracture
warning was issued. Therefore, the early warning system achieved a 100% success rate
in the experiment.
To clearly explain the specific criteria for successful early warning, we have
supplemented the Methods section of the manuscript with the following explanation:
(lines 1061-1076): "Criteria for determining successful warning".
<Reviewer 2>: 5. In the “Methods: Preparation of test specimens and experimental
procedures” section, the reviewer notes that the loading grips and fixtures are likely
made of ferromagnetic materials. Additionally, large instruments in the surrounding
environment may generate ambient magnetic fields. Could these factors affect the test
results?
Response:
During fatigue testing, the loading fixtures and clamping devices-composed of
ferromagnetic materials-may generate ambient magnetic fields. However, their
influence on experimental results is negligible. Moreover, owing to its inherent self-
compensation capability, MagDrift can effectively suppress these ambient interferences.
To verify this, we conducted the following supplementary experiments:
Magnetic strength wave test analysis under no load conditions
To further discuss the impact of the loading device on the test results, we
supplemented the magnetic strength fluctuation exploration tests under no-load
conditions (without test specimens on the testing machine). This divided into two cases:
with and without magnets. The lower fixture was vibrated 20,000 times at a frequency
of 20 Hz to simulate the actual fatigue loading process. The changes in magnetic
strength and displacement during the test are shown in Fig. 18.
As can be seen from the figure, since no test specimen was placed on the testing
machine, the magnetic strength and displacement exhibit a linear trend, and no
significant fluctuations can be observed with the naked eye. By fitting the equations
describing the changes in magnetic strength under the two conditions, it was found that
the slopes of the magnetic strength fitting equations were -5.17581E-9 (with magnet,
without specimen) and 1.63773E-7 (without magnet, without specimen), respectively.
These values are far smaller than the changes in magnetic field strength observed during
normal fatigue cycle loading tests.
Furthermore, due to the self-compensating properties of MagDrift during data
processing, these minor fluctuations exert only a negligible impact on the experimental
results.
Fig. 18. Changes in magnetic strength and displacement under no-load conditions. a, with
magnet, without specimen. b, without magnet, without specimen.
Magnetic strength wave test analysis without magnet but with specimen
To highlight the rigor of the test data, we also supplemented the magnetic strength
fluctuation exploration tests under test without the applied magnets but with a specimen
installed. We analyzed the magnetic strength fluctuations upper and lower the test piece
under empty magnetic conditions. We selected a standard soft magnetic iron piece and
conducted a fatigue loading test at 485 MPa without adding magnets. The test results
are shown in Fig. 19.
As can be seen from the figure, the displacement change is no different from that
in a normal fatigue test, but the fluctuations in magnetic strength remain imperceptible
to the naked eye throughout the entire process. We also fitted the trends of magnetic
strength changes at the two positions and found that the slopes of the equations
describing the trends in magnetic strength changes at the upper and lower positions
were -2.30467E-8 (upper magnetic strength) and -1.15808E-9 (lower magnetic
strength), respectively. These values are still far smaller than the magnetic strength
trend changes observed during normal fatigue loading processes.
Based on the two supplementary experiments, it can be concluded that the
magnetic field generated by the experimental setup has a negligible impact on the
experimental results. Moreover, the representative metric used in this study-MagDrift-
demonstrates inherent self-compensation characteristics, effectively canceling out or
mitigating interference from ambient magnetic fields. As a result, minor magnetic
fluctuations originating from the experimental apparatus have negligible influence on
the reliability of the experimental outcomes.

<Reviewer 2>: 6. Also in this section, the authors mention using five N35 magnets.
Please clarify whether these are permanent magnets, specify the initial magnetic field
strength they generate, and explain the rationale for choosing this level of excitation.
Response:
The primary reason for selecting five N35 magnets as the external magnetic
excitation is that during the fatigue process of the material, the change in magnetic
strength under this initial magnetic strength can maximize the fatigue signal, ensuring
that the change in magnetic strength under this condition can reflect the fatigue
characteristics of the material itself. To elaborate more clearly on the reasons for
choosing this external magnetic excitation, we have supplemented the following
experimental and theoretical analysis:
Analysis of notched bar magnetic saturation test
The experiment utilized N35 neodymium-iron-boron permanent magnets. The
initial surface magnetic field strength of a stack of five N35 magnets measured between
240 and 250 mT. Multiple calibrations were performed using a gauss meter to ensure
data reproducibility. To justify the use of this external magnetic excitation, a
supplementary comparative experiment was conducted to evaluate variations in the
saturation magnetic field strength of test specimens under different external magnetic
excitations and crack depths. The specific experimental procedure is detailed below.
The experiment used an iron rod measuring 16 mm in diameter and 25 cm in length,
and employed neodymium-iron-boron magnets to apply eight distinct levels of external
magnetic field excitation: 50 mT, 87 mT, 124 mT, 158 mT, 185 mT, 211 mT, 317 mT,
and 430 mT.
Select the midpoint of the iron rod (at 12.5 cm) as the preset crack point. When
setting the preset crack, the crack width is 1 mm. When the crack depth is less than 10
mm, the cutting depth is 2 mm each time. After exceeding 10 mm, the cutting depth is
1 mm each time until the crack depth reaches 15 mm.
Select four measuring points at 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm, and 20 cm along the length
direction of the iron rod. Use a handheld gauss meter to collect magnetic strength at the
measuring points at a lifting height of 3 mm. The experimental setup and data are shown
in Fig. 20.
Fig. 20. Schematic diagram of the comprehensive relationship between magnetic strength
changes at different measuring points and under different crack depths under different
external magnetic excitations. a, Schematic diagram of notched bar magnetic saturation test and
external magnetic field configuration location. The preset crack position is located at the geometric
center of the test piece, with measuring points 1 and 2 located in front of the crack, and measuring
points 3 and 4 located behind the crack. The external magnetic field is applied by neodymium-iron-
boron permanent magnets, covering eight excitation levels from 50–430 mT. b, Schematic diagram
of finite element simulation of crack depth on magnetic induction line distribution. When there are
cracks in the material, the magnetic flux in the damaged area at the crack location section decreases,
while the magnetic flux in the undamaged area increases accordingly; and the increase in crack
depth leads to an increase in magnetic flux in the undamaged area. c, The evolution law of magnetic
strength at each measuring point under eight types of external magnetic excitation as a function of
crack depth. As the external magnetic excitation increases, the magnetic strength at each measuring
point increases synchronously. When the crack depth reaches a corresponding value, there is a trend
of increasing magnetic strength at measuring points in front of the crack and decreasing magnetic
strength at measuring points behind the crack. d, Output the relationship diagram between the
acceleration of magnetic field changes and the remaining depth, external magnetic excitation, and
the ratio of magnetic excitation to undamaged area.
Exploration of saturation magnetic strength of iron rods with different crack
depths
The experimental results indicate that when the measurement point is ahead of the
crack, the magnetic field intensity initially increases slowly and then at an accelerating
rate as the crack deepens; when the point is behind the crack, the intensity first decreases
slowly and then at an accelerating rate. The underlying physical mechanism can be
described as follows: Cracks force magnetic field lines to divert around intact regions.
When the magnetic permeability in these regions remains unsaturated, the magnetic
flux continues to vary gradually. As a result, the magnetic field intensity initially
exhibits a slow decreasing or increasing trend as crack depth increases. With further
crack propagation and increased external magnetic excitation, the local magnetic
permeability-particularly at the most vulnerable cross-section-begins transitioning from
an unsaturated to a saturated state. Once the magnetic circuit around the crack reaches
saturation, the permeability in the region behind the crack decreases significantly,
leading to a pronounced decline in magnetic field intensity. Simultaneously, due to the
concentration of magnetic flux ahead of the crack, the magnetic strength in this zone
demonstrates a marked increasing trend.
We analyzed the remaining cross-sectional undamaged ratio when the magnetic
strength reached saturation under different external excitation magnetic intensities, as
shown in Table. 2.

saturation under different excitation magnetic intensities.

Analysis of the data presented in Table 2 revealed a linear relationship between
the intensity of the external magnetic excitation and the ratio of the undamaged area.
The slope of the linear fit was determined to be 0.011, which serves as a quantitative
measure of both the crack damage extent and the external magnetic excitation intensity
under critical saturation conditions.
Analysis of the residual thickness in the crack region at magnetic saturation under
varying external magnetic excitation intensities reveals that when the residual section
depth is 8 mm, the external excitation magnetic field begins to enter the saturation-
critical transition zone within an approximate range of 211–317 mT. According to the
specification (GB/T 3075-2021) for fatigue loading tests, the diameter of the clamped
end of a curved specimen shall be more than twice the diameter of the thinnest section
in the middle. Given that the clamped end diameter of the specimen is 16 mm, the
minimum thickness at the midsection is taken as 8 mm (analogous to a residual depth
of 8 mm). At this residual depth, an external magnetic excitation intensity of 240–250
mT corresponds accurately to the median value of the magnetic saturation-critical
transition zone.
The fatigue test therefore employs an external magnetic excitation of 240–250 mT.
This intensity not only sufficiently amplifies the fatigue signal but also effectively
isolates geometric effects, thereby highlighting the intrinsic evolution of material
fatigue and ensuring the dominance of the material's fatigue-related response. This
consideration is a key rationale for selecting a stack of five N35 magnets as the external
magnetic excitation source in this experiment.

<Reviewer 2>: 8. When measuring the magnetic field, the Hall sensor is placed beneath
the specimen. Why was this location selected? Although the manuscript states that a
linear relationship exists between magnetic changes measured at the remote end and
the variation in binding force at the weakest section, the specimen is not of uniform
cylindrical geometry. Is this assumption still valid in the given configuration?
Response:
The paper places the Hall sensor beneath the specimen, mainly based strategic
sensor placement designed to optimally capture changes in magnetic flux, to ensure that
the magnetic flux changes caused by cracks can be directly and efficiently captured;
The paper adopts MagDrift as the core indicator, effectively eliminating the nonlinear
errors caused by non-uniform geometry of the sample, sensor position differences, and
environmental interference, thereby ensuring the reliability of the linear relationship
between macroscopic magnetic flux and microscopic bonding force changes in non-
uniform cylindrical samples. We have supplemented theoretical analysis and fatigue
tests at different locations to fully illustrate this issue.
Analysis of sensor layout selection based on accurately capturing magnetic flux
changes
During the process of fatigue crack propagation, magnetic field lines will undergo
significant changes at the fracture surface. Placing the sensor beneath the specimen can
maximize the capture efficiency of magnetic signal changes caused by fatigue fracture.
During the fatigue process of materials, the magnetic domain structure inside the
material will undergo distortion, resulting in the redistribution of local magnetic flux
fields. If the fracture surface is placed on the magnet sensor connection, the magnetic
flux change generated by the crack can directly and unobstructed penetrate the sensitive
area of the sensor, thereby maximizing the efficiency of capturing magnetic flux change
signals. This avoids magnetic flux attenuation or scattering caused by positional
deviation, significantly improving the sensitivity and accuracy of detection.
In addition, the MagDrift data measured under this deployment strategy can
respond in real-time to weak fatigue characteristic changes, providing a solid physical
foundation for fatigue failure warning and ensuring the high reliability of experimental
data.
Fatigue loading test in different positions of sensors
Regarding the influence of sensor position on the magnetic signal, it can be
observed from previous comparative experiments on magnetic strength changes at
different measurement points under varying crack depths that: when the sensor is
positioned ahead of the crack, the magnetic field strength at the measurement point
initially remains stable and then increases; when the sensor is located behind the crack,
the magnetic field strength initially remains stable and then decreases.
We have supplemented the fatigue loading tests of the sensor at different positions,
and the magnetic strength change rate and strain are shown in Fig. 25, while the
MagDrift change is shown in Fig. 26.
It can be seen that when the fatigue fracture position is below the specimen and
the sensor is arranged above the fracture position, the magnetic strength shows an
upward trend and the MagDrift shows a downward trend. When the fatigue fracture
location is above the specimen and the sensor is arranged below the fracture location,
the magnetic strength shows a downward trend and the MagDrift shows an upward
trend. Both MagDrift and magnetic strength change rates show opposite trends. This is
also in line with the previous notched bar magnetic saturation test.
Fig. 25. CRMS and strain of the sensor Fig. 26. MagDrift and peak to peak of
above and below the specimen under fatigue displacement of the sensor above and below
loading. the specimen under fatigue loading.
MagDrift mitigate the effects of nonlinearities
We established a relationship between the macroscopic magnetic flux change and
the variation in bonding force at the weakest cross-section based on the assumption of
small deformation. During actual fatigue loading tests, higher-order terms, sensor
position and distance, material inhomogeneity, and other factors may lead to
nonlinearities in the experimental data. Furthermore, as demonstrated by the
experimental validation and theoretical analysis above, the geometric inhomogeneity
of the material or changes in the fracture location indeed affect the magnetic field
variation, but their primary influence is on the absolute measured values of the magnetic
field strength. In this paper, the core indicator used to characterize the material's fatigue
performance is not the absolute magnetic field strength, but rather MagDrift, which is
adopted as the representative parameter for characterizing the material's fatigue
behavior.
The key advantage of MagDrift is to offset or reduce the influence of factors such
as non-uniformity of test materials, positional differences, environmental interference,
or test equipment on magnetic strength values by calculating peak to peak values.
And MagDrift has inherent self-compensation characteristics, which effectively reduces
measurement system errors compared to the absolute value of magnetic strength.
Therefore, even if the sample is not a uniform cylindrical structure. In this configuration,
the underlying assumption of the model remains valid.
<Reviewer 2>: 9. Building upon the previous question: does the location of fatigue
fracture affect the intensity of the measured magnetic signal?
Response:
The specific location of fatigue fracture only affects the absolute value of magnetic
strength, but the influence of this positional difference can be effectively eliminated by
the relative change rate of magnetic strength. This ensures that the fatigue performance
evolution of the material can still be stably and reliably characterized at different
fracture locations. We have added the following content to elaborate on this issue in
detail:
Analysis of magnetic signal variations due to different fracture positions in
notched bar magnetic saturation test
As demonstrated in the previous notched bar magnetic saturation test (Fig. 20),
when the fatigue fracture occurs beyond the magnet-sensor connection zone, the
magnetic field strength at the measurement point initially increases slowly and then
accelerates as the crack propagates. In contrast, when the fracture is located within the
magnet-sensor connection zone, the magnetic field strength exhibits an initial slow
decrease followed by an accelerated decline. These results confirm that the location of
fatigue fracture significantly influences the variation trend of magnetic signals.
Fatigue loading tests at different fracture locations
The notched bar magnetic saturation test explored the influence of different
fracture positions on the change trend of magnetic signal under static conditions. In
order to analyze the influence of different fracture positions on the change of magnetic
strength during the fatigue loading test, we supplemented the fatigue loading test under
different sensor positions (the change rate of magnetic strength and strain are shown in
Fig. 25 above, and the MagDrift is shown in Fig. 26).
From the experimental data, it can be seen that the change in magnetic strength
when the fatigue fracture location is within the connection between the magnet and the
sensor is opposite to the change in magnetic strength when it is outside the connection
between the magnet and the sensor, and the MagDrift also shows opposite trends in
both cases.
The opposite trend of change corresponds to the magnetic strength variation
observed in the previous notched bar magnetic saturation test. When the fracture
location is outside the connection between the sensor and the magnet, the magnetic
strength shows an upward trend, and when the fracture location is inside the connection
between the sensor and the magnet, the magnetic strength shows a downward trend.
Representative indicator - MagDrift
From fatigue tests at different fracture locations, it can be seen that it mainly
affects the absolute measurement value of magnetic strength. However, the core
indicator used in this study to characterize the fatigue performance of materials is not
the absolute magnetic field strength value, but rather the use of MagDrift as a
representative indicator to characterize the fatigue performance of materials. Compared
to the absolute value of magnetic strength, MagDrift can effectively counteract or
weaken the effects caused by differences in fracture location. And MagDrift has
inherent self-compensation characteristics, effectively reducing system measurement
errors, etc.
<Reviewer 2>: 10. In the “Fatigue Fracture Early Warning Algorithm” section, the
alarm mechanism needs to be more thoroughly explained. At minimum, the following
points should be clarified:
(1) What is the physical meaning of the two selected formulas?
(2) What is the physical meaning of S₁ in the equations?
(3) Describe the computational procedure in detail, including whether the method
is applicable only after 90% of the fatigue life has elapsed, and whether a moving
window is employed during prediction.
Response:
The two warning formulas proposed in the paper have clear physical meanings,
mainly targeting the accelerated damage mutation of low cycle fatigue and the gradual
damage accumulation mechanism of high cycle fatigue. By capturing the mutation
characteristics of MagDrift, the degradation state of the weakest section bonding force
and material fatigue performance can be determined. The warning calculation adopts a
dynamic dual moving window mechanism to dynamically slide and update data in real
time, without relying on fatigue life percentage. Its essence is to capture the sudden
change characteristics of MagDrift and achieve the purpose of warning. The following
will elaborate in detail from three aspects: MagDrift mutation mechanism, parameter
definition, and warning dynamic window algorithm:
Mechanism of MagDrift fracture mutation - saturation magnetic strength critical
effect
Our warning algorithm is predicated on a physical model inspired by the magnetic
saturation behavior observed in our supplementary bar-cutting tests.
In the notched bar magnetic saturation test, we systematically explored the
influence of crack depth on magnetic strength evolution under different external
magnetic excitations of 50-430 mT. The magnetic saturation law of ferromagnetic
materials during damage propagation was revealed by setting different crack depths of
2-15 mm and measuring the magnetic strength at measuring points. The core conclusion
of this experiment is that under different external magnetic excitations, when the critical
value of magnetic saturation is reached at the crack, the local magnetic permeability of
the material will enter a saturated state, leading to accelerated increase and decrease in
magnetic strength in the pre and post crack regions, respectively. This is due to the fact
that magnetic field lines are forced to orbit undamaged areas, and the initial changes in
magnetic flux are gentle; But once the crack reaches a saturated magnetic strength state,
the magnetic flux distortion significantly intensifies. For a detailed explanation, please
refer to <Reviewer 2>: 6.
In fatigue testing, the accumulation of material fatigue damage is analogous to the
deepening process of cracks in cutting tests. For example, the sudden change point of
MagDrift is directly related to the achievement of the "saturation magnetic strength
critical state".
During fatigue testing, when the material is in the early to mid-stages of fatigue
damage, microcracks propagate gradually while the magnetic circuit remains
unsaturated. Under these conditions, the variation in MagDrift exhibits a stable and
moderate trend, consistent with the gentle variation observed in magnetic field strength
at the measurement point under non-saturated conditions during the notched bar
magnetic saturation test.
When the material accumulates fatigue damage and is about to fracture, the
MagDrift change begins to undergo a sudden change, and the magnetic strength at the
weakest section reaches a state of magnetic saturation. This is analogous to the
accelerated change in magnetic strength at the measuring point when the crack position
in the steel cutting test is about to reach saturation magnetic strength.
At this point, if the loading continues, the material will experience fatigue fracture,
and the MagDrift will show a sudden rise or fall trend, which is similar to the
acceleration of the magnetic strength at the measuring point after reaching saturation in
the notched bar magnetic saturation test.
Therefore, we hypothesize that the sudden change in MagDrift signifies a critical
shift in the material's magnetic state, potentially analogous to the approach to magnetic
saturation at a microscopic flaw. This critical transition, informed by the static bar-
cutting experiments, serves as the physical basis for our warning algorithm.

Lifetime applicability and dynamic window mechanism
This method is not limited to being applicable only after the material's fatigue life
reaches 90%. This warning algorithm mainly utilizes the dual moving window
algorithm to dynamically slide and update data in real time, which can cover the entire
fatigue life cycle. The essence of the warning algorithm is to capture the mutation
characteristics of MagDrift and achieve the purpose of warning, regardless of the
percentage of fatigue life. Four consecutive triggers ensure the elimination of
interference from instantaneous MagDrift changes.
